For the typical person it acts on (a 35-year-old White woman born in the United States, never married and not living in a family, a high-school graduate in an administrative or clerical job in the private sector, working 40 hours a week), it slightly raises the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, from about 97% to about 98% (on the training data only).
Through it, being a woman clearly raises a typical person's predicted chance from about 61% to about 73%.
Private household service clearly raises it even more for women: from about 73% to about 99% for a woman, and from about 61% to about 95% for a man.
Through this part, private household service raises it from about 61% to about 92% (on the training data only).

For the typical woman it acts on, capital gains barely and only slightly change it, staying at about 98% from 0 to 6849 US dollars, flattening out near the top because the predicted chance cannot go much higher (on the training data only).

ann_125.text: Through this part, a higher education level and higher capital losses clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less steadily: from about 79% at 7 to about 38% at 13 on the 1-16 scale, and from about 61% at 0 to about 30% at 1887 US dollars.

Being other than a husband or wife in the household clearly raises it to about 91%, farming or fishing to about 87%, other service work to about 86%, not living in a family to about 84% and being never married to about 82%.
Being older and working longer hours clearly lower it steadily: from about 69% at 22 to about 47% at 58 years, and from about 71% at 24 to about 50% at 55 hours a week.

A higher education level and higher capital losses also clearly lower it steadily: from about 79% at 7 to about 38% at 13 on the 1-16 scale, and from about 61% at 0 to about 30% at 1887 US dollars.

Compared with a husband in a professional job, working in private household service clearly raises it to about 95%, being other than a husband or wife in the household to about 91%, farming or fishing to about 87%, other service work to about 86% and not living in a family to about 84%.

Being never married rather than married clearly raises it to about 82%, being separated to about 78% and being a woman to about 73%, while being a wife rather than a husband clearly lowers it to about 36%.
Being older and working longer hours clearly lower it steadily: from about 69% at 22 to about 47% at 58 years, and from about 71% at 24 to about 50% at 55 hours a week.

Being born in Colombia raises it to about 99% and in the Dominican Republic to about 79%, being born in Portugal lowers it to about 39%, and a missing work class raises it to about 78% (on the training data only).
Working without pay raises it to above 99% and being born in Laos to about 86% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this: only 17 people each).

ann_116.original: Capital-gain (standardised; output is P(income<=50K)) enters the logit as a convex piecewise-linear decreasing function: a direct linear term -2.658*cg (via idn_o63) plus a ReLU hinge -0.364*relu(1.161*cg-0.500) that steepens the slope from -2.66 to -3.08 above cg~0.43 SD (raw ~$4.3k; ~5.7% of rows). Large capital gains push strongly towards >50K. Evidence (train, 39,073 rows): closed form verified by get_formula; viz summaries confirm the exits; mean-ablating this leaf's logit contribution gives acc 0.8359 / AUC 0.8877 (baseline 0.8518 / 0.9056), mean |dP| 0.0624, max |dP| 0.997. Removing only the hinge (keeping the linear term) barely changes performance (AUC 0.9054): the capital-gain effect is mostly linear in the standardised value.
ann_116.proposed: This part clearly lowers the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less as capital gains rise, from about 61% to about 11% at 6849 US dollars.

ann_117.original: ReLU gate 369 = relu(-0.869*sex + 0.243*occupation:9 - 0.0053*relu(1.161*cg-0.5) - 0.540), read out with +0.863. sex=1 (male) closes the gate unless occupation:9 (Priv-house-serv) is set; for women it is open (~0.68) and adds ~+0.58 logit towards <=50K, Priv-house-serv adds a further ~+3 logit. The capital-gain path (816_b) has a negligible weight. Evidence (train, 39,073 rows): closed form verified by get_formula; viz summaries confirm the exits; mean-ablating this leaf's logit contribution gives acc 0.8511 / AUC 0.9039 (baseline 0.8518 / 0.9056), mean |dP| 0.0237, max |dP| 0.618. Mean 369 by cell: female 0.676, female+Priv-house-serv 4.20, male 0, male+Priv-house-serv 2.36. Dropping the capital-gain path changes 369 by at most 0.078.
ann_117.proposed: This part clearly raises the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less for women, and private household service clearly raises it further, even more so for women.

ann_118.original: workclass:0 ('?', unknown workclass; 5.7% of rows) feeds two ReLUs: 2098 (always active, +0.45 readout) and 4158 (active only when workclass='?', -0.368 readout). Since the input is binary, together they form a single category offset: +0.82 logit towards <=50K when workclass is unknown. Evidence (train, 39,073 rows): closed form verified by get_formula; viz summaries confirm the exits; mean-ablating this leaf's logit contribution gives acc 0.8510 / AUC 0.9050 (baseline 0.8518 / 0.9056), mean |dP| 0.0072, max |dP| 0.191.

ann_119.original: workclass:8 (Without-pay, 17 training rows) passes through an always-active ReLU 5203 (readout +1.098) plus a direct term (idn_o10). On the rare standardised value (~48) the sum is ~+61 logit: an override that forces the prediction to <=50K for unpaid workers; ~0 effect otherwise. ann_119.proposed: This part raises the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less to above 99% for people who work without pay (on the training data only; the model has little data on this, with 17 people).

ann_126.original: Root: P(income<=50K) = sigmoid(0.808 + linear_backbone + capital_gain_hinge + female_or_household_gate + 7 single-category offsets). Composition is purely additive in logit space; the children never feed each other. Category offsets (train logit deltas): unknown workclass +0.82, Without-pay +61 (override to <=50K, 17 rows), Exec-managerial -0.82, Wife -2.90, Japan +0.14 (two large near-cancelling terms), Separated +0.23, dead Private unit 0. Since every bump has a single binary input, each is exactly an affine function of that indicator; the network is therefore a logistic regression plus two genuine nonlinearities: a convex capital-gain hinge (slope -2.66 -> -3.08 above ~0.43 SD) and an OR-like ReLU gate that adds +0.58 logit for women and +2 to +3.6 logit for Priv-house-serv. 56 unconnected inputs are zero-effect entries. Evidence (train, 39,073 rows): acc 0.852, AUC 0.906. Mean-ablation AUC drops: linear_backbone 0.906->0.753, capital_gain_hinge ->0.888, wife_bump ->0.887, exec_managerial ->0.903, female gate ->0.904; others <0.001. SHAP (500 rows) top: relationship:0 Husband, education-num, capital-gain, Married-civ-spouse, Wife, Exec-managerial, age, hours-per-week, relationship:1, sex.
ann_126.proposed: The whole model adds up separate effects: capital gains, a higher education level and capital losses clearly lower the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less; private household service, not being a husband or wife, and being a woman clearly raise it, private household service even more so for women.

summary.text: For a typical person (a 37-year-old White married man born in the United States, a high-school graduate in a professional job in the private sector, working 40 hours a week, with no capital gains or losses), the model predicts about a 61% chance of an income of $50,000 or less, and higher capital gains clearly lower that steadily: from about 61% at none to about 11% at 6849 US dollars, a large change, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.

A higher education level and higher capital losses clearly lower the predicted chance steadily: from about 79% at 7 to about 38% at 13 on the 1-16 scale, and from about 61% at no capital losses to about 30% at 1887 US dollars.
Working in private household service clearly raises it to about 95%, and being other than a husband or wife in the household to about 91%.
Private household service clearly raises it even more for women: for a typical person, from about 73% to about 99% for a woman, and from about 61% to about 95% for a man.
A higher census sampling weight slightly lowers it steadily, from about 62% at 66,572 to about 58% at 328,216 (on the training data only).

parts.name: full_model
parts.original_hypothesis: Root: P(income<=50K) = sigmoid(0.808 + linear_backbone + capital_gain_hinge + female_or_household_gate + 7 single-category offsets). Composition is purely additive in logit space; the children never feed each other. Category offsets (train logit deltas): unknown workclass +0.82, Without-pay +61 (override to <=50K, 17 rows), Exec-managerial -0.82, Wife -2.90, Japan +0.14 (two large near-cancelling terms), Separated +0.23, dead Private unit 0. Since every bump has a single binary input, each is exactly an affine function of that indicator; the network is therefore a logistic regression plus two genuine nonlinearities: a convex capital-gain hinge (slope -2.66 -> -3.08 above ~0.43 SD) and an OR-like ReLU gate that adds +0.58 logit for women and +2 to +3.6 logit for Priv-house-serv. 56 unconnected inputs are zero-effect entries. Evidence (train, 39,073 rows): acc 0.852, AUC 0.906. Mean-ablation AUC drops: linear_backbone 0.906->0.753, capital_gain_hinge ->0.888, wife_bump ->0.887, exec_managerial ->0.903, female gate ->0.904; others <0.001. SHAP (500 rows) top: relationship:0 Husband, education-num, capital-gain, Married-civ-spouse, Wife, Exec-managerial, age, hours-per-week, relationship:1, sex.

parts.name: capital_gain_hinge
parts.original_hypothesis: Capital-gain (standardised; output is P(income<=50K)) enters the logit as a convex piecewise-linear decreasing function: a direct linear term -2.658*cg (via idn_o63) plus a ReLU hinge -0.364*relu(1.161*cg-0.500) that steepens the slope from -2.66 to -3.08 above cg~0.43 SD (raw ~$4.3k; ~5.7% of rows). Large capital gains push strongly towards >50K. Evidence (train, 39,073 rows): closed form verified by get_formula; viz summaries confirm the exits; mean-ablating this leaf's logit contribution gives acc 0.8359 / AUC 0.8877 (baseline 0.8518 / 0.9056), mean |dP| 0.0624, max |dP| 0.997. Removing only the hinge (keeping the linear term) barely changes performance (AUC 0.9054): the capital-gain effect is mostly linear in the standardised value.

parts.name: linear_backbone
parts.original_hypothesis: Sparse linear backbone: 41 inputs each add a single weighted term, summed at identity node lin_agg (std 1.99 logit on train). Dominant terms (output = P(<=50K)): relationship:0 Husband -0.93, education-num -0.78, hours-per-week -0.36, age -0.36, marital-status:2 Married-civ-spouse -0.31, relationship:1 -0.29, capital-loss -0.27, occupation:8 Other-service +0.25, marital-status:4 Never-married +0.24. native-country:15 is constant on train (acts as a bias). Evidence (train, 39,073 rows): closed form verified by get_formula; viz summaries confirm the exits; mean-ablating this leaf's logit contribution gives acc 0.8023 / AUC 0.7529 (baseline 0.8518 / 0.9056), mean |dP| 0.1587, max |dP| 0.907.

parts.name: without_pay_override
parts.original_hypothesis: workclass:8 (Without-pay, 17 training rows) passes through an always-active ReLU 5203 (readout +1.098) plus a direct term (idn_o10). On the rare standardised value (~48) the sum is ~+61 logit: an override that forces the prediction to <=50K for unpaid workers; ~0 effect otherwise. Evidence (train, 39,073 rows): closed form verified by get_formula; viz summaries confirm the exits; mean-ablating this leaf's logit contribution gives acc 0.8518 / AUC 0.9057 (baseline 0.8518 / 0.9056), mean |dP| 0.0027, max |dP| 0.533.

parts.name: wife_bump
parts.original_hypothesis: relationship:5 (Wife, 4.9% of rows) acts via a direct term (idn_o56, -0.531), and a two-ReLU serial chain 5009 -> 1579 where 1579 opens only for wives (readout -1.043). Net offset: -2.90 logit towards >50K for wives (complementing the direct Husband term in the linear backbone). Evidence (train, 39,073 rows): closed form verified by get_formula; viz summaries confirm the exits; mean-ablating this leaf's logit contribution gives acc 0.8450 / AUC 0.8868 (baseline 0.8518 / 0.9056), mean |dP| 0.0295, max |dP| 0.598.

parts.name: female_or_household_gate
parts.original_hypothesis: ReLU gate 369 = relu(-0.869*sex + 0.243*occupation:9 - 0.0053*relu(1.161*cg-0.5) - 0.540), read out with +0.863. sex=1 (male) closes the gate unless occupation:9 (Priv-house-serv) is set; for women it is open (~0.68) and adds ~+0.58 logit towards <=50K, Priv-house-serv adds a further ~+3 logit. The capital-gain path (816_b) has a negligible weight. Evidence (train, 39,073 rows): closed form verified by get_formula; viz summaries confirm the exits; mean-ablating this leaf's logit contribution gives acc 0.8511 / AUC 0.9039 (baseline 0.8518 / 0.9056), mean |dP| 0.0237, max |dP| 0.618. Mean 369 by cell: female 0.676, female+Priv-house-serv 4.20, male 0, male+Priv-house-serv 2.36. Dropping the capital-gain path changes 369 by at most 0.078.

parts.name: exec_managerial_bump
parts.original_hypothesis: occupation:4 (Exec-managerial, 12.4% of rows) has a direct term (idn_o45) plus a ReLU 2058 active only for managers (readout -0.27). Net category offset: -0.82 logit, i.e. towards >50K for managers. Evidence (train, 39,073 rows): closed form verified by get_formula; viz summaries confirm the exits; mean-ablating this leaf's logit contribution gives acc 0.8481 / AUC 0.9025 (baseline 0.8518 / 0.9056), mean |dP| 0.0205, max |dP| 0.177.

parts.name: unknown_workclass_bump
parts.original_hypothesis: workclass:0 ('?', unknown workclass; 5.7% of rows) feeds two ReLUs: 2098 (always active, +0.45 readout) and 4158 (active only when workclass='?', -0.368 readout). Since the input is binary, together they form a single category offset: +0.82 logit towards <=50K when workclass is unknown. Evidence (train, 39,073 rows): closed form verified by get_formula; viz summaries confirm the exits; mean-ablating this leaf's logit contribution gives acc 0.8510 / AUC 0.9050 (baseline 0.8518 / 0.9056), mean |dP| 0.0072, max |dP| 0.191.

parts.name: separated_bump
parts.original_hypothesis: marital-status:5 (Separated, 3.2% of rows) passes through an always-active ReLU 1009 (readout +0.201); linear in the binary input. Net offset +0.23 logit towards <=50K for separated people. Evidence (train, 39,073 rows): closed form verified by get_formula; viz summaries confirm the exits; mean-ablating this leaf's logit contribution gives acc 0.8519 / AUC 0.9056 (baseline 0.8518 / 0.9056), mean |dP| 0.0010, max |dP| 0.055.

parts.name: japan_cancelling_bump
parts.original_hypothesis: native-country:24 (Japan, 68 rows) feeds an always-active ReLU 6081 (readout +0.205, ~+4.7 logit on the rare value) and a direct term (idn_o83, ~-4.6 logit). The two nearly cancel: net offset +0.14 logit for Japan-born. Effectively a small category offset. Evidence (train, 39,073 rows): closed form verified by get_formula; viz summaries confirm the exits; mean-ablating this leaf's logit contribution gives acc 0.8517 / AUC 0.9056 (baseline 0.8518 / 0.9056), mean |dP| 0.0000, max |dP| 0.034.

parts.name: dead_private_unit
parts.original_hypothesis: workclass:4 (Private) feeds ReLU 6764 = relu(1.0*wc4 - 0.683). The standardised input never exceeds 0.662, so the unit is always 0 on the training data (dead unit): this subgraph contributes nothing. Evidence (train, 39,073 rows): closed form verified by get_formula; viz summaries confirm the exits; mean-ablating this leaf's logit contribution gives acc 0.8518 / AUC 0.9056 (baseline 0.8518 / 0.9056), mean |dP| 0.0000, max |dP| 0.000.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording
